We sometimes take it for granted that a whole will turn out as good as each of its individual parts. Imagine, for instance, that you run a startup and that every person you have hired is productive and efficient. It may look logical to conclude that the startup itself will therefore be productive and efficient — but that does not necessarily follow. The fallacy of composition overlooks how the separate parts interact with one another. If your skilled administrator and your expert head of IT each assume the other will compile the test results, no one does, and trouble arises. In the same way, a team of talented people can still pursue a doomed project, and a project full of good ideas can lack a stable core. Strong individuals, in short, do not automatically add up to a strong whole. So when building a team, examine the overall picture as carefully as the individuals. The interaction among the parts is what ultimately decides the outcome.
①how to recruit only the most productive and efficient employees
②the importance of assigning clear job titles within a startup
③why a strong whole cannot be guaranteed merely by strong individual parts
④why small teams outperform large teams on creative projects
⑤how good ideas naturally lead to financially successful projects

Humans are remarkably good at picturing things in the mind's eye. Our brains evolved this ability so that we could rehearse upcoming actions internally, without the risks of trying them out in reality. Brain-imaging studies even suggest that imagining a scene activates many of the same regions as actually seeing it. Yet evolution has made sure that these inner images are never quite as vivid as the real thing. This limitation is not a flaw but a built-in safeguard. If imagining a feast satisfied your hunger as fully as eating one, you would have no reason to look for real food. You would simply imagine yourself dining and slowly starve. So our mental pictures stay deliberately less authentic, keeping us motivated to act in the real world.

For every objective probability, from one percent to one hundred percent, we can ask what subjective weight people assign to it. When we make decisions, do we treat a one-percent chance as exactly one percent, or as something larger? Events that are possible but unlikely — say, probabilities up to about twenty-five percent — count as low-probability events. Such events tend to influence our decisions more than they objectively should. An event with a true one-percent chance can feel, subjectively, like a five-percent chance. In other words, we overestimate how likely these rare events are. As a rule, the smaller the actual probability, the more we exaggerate it. Lottery players, for instance, stay hopeful even though the odds against them are astronomical.

②our tendency to overestimate the likelihood of low-probability events
③why people enjoy taking risks more as they grow older
④how advertising manipulates consumers into buying lottery tickets
⑤the difference between objective and subjective measurement tools

Trade is often held back not by a shortage of buyers or markets, but by the difficulty of delivering goods to those markets at competitive prices. For firms, transaction costs are far from trivial: beyond the direct cost of exchange, there are the costs of converting, paying, and hedging money simply to settle for goods and services. When several countries share a single currency, many of these transaction costs vanish. The money once wasted on conversion can then be channeled back into a firm's productivity and innovation. In effect, unproductive costs are transformed into productive investment, yielding long-term gains for the entire economy. By uniting their currencies, economies tend to grow more than they ever could while standing alone. A shared currency thus lays a firm economic foundation from which everyone can benefit. The advantage is not confined to a single firm but spreads across whole economies.

②how cultural differences slow down international trade agreements
③the reasons companies prefer cash payments over digital transfers
④how a shared currency lowers costs and fuels broad economic growth
⑤the historical origins of money in early trading societies

Even the light from our nearest stellar neighbor needs four years to travel to our eyes. So whenever we gaze at the stars, we are really looking back into time. This is an extraordinary gift, for we glimpse parts of the universe as they appeared long ago. The farther away the light we gather, the deeper into the past we are able to see. Look at Betelgeuse, glowing in the constellation Orion, and you wind the clock back more than six hundred years. Its reddish light began its journey toward Earth during the Middle Ages. The stars of Orion's belt lie even farther off, their light having traveled at least a thousand years to reach us. Because of this, the night sky gives us a chance to understand the history of the universe itself.

Jacob Lawrence was an American painter celebrated for his vivid depictions of African-American history and everyday life. Born in Atlantic City in 1917, he moved to Harlem at the age of thirteen and studied art at the Utopia Children's Center. In his paintings he favored bright colors and simplified shapes. The Migration Series, widely regarded as his masterpiece, brought him national recognition. During World War II he served in the U.S. Coast Guard and created many paintings, though most of them were lost. He later taught at the University of Washington for sixteen years. Over the course of his life he received honorary degrees from several universities, including Harvard. Until just a few weeks before his death, he continued to explore the lives of African-Americans through his art.

The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead argued that civilization advances by increasing the number of operations we can perform without thinking about them. The discount coupon is a good example of such an 'advance,' since it lets shoppers assume that presenting it will lower their purchase price. How mechanically we act on that assumption was revealed by the experience of one automobile-tire company. Because of a printing error, some mailed coupons offered no savings at all, yet they drew just as much customer response as the valid ones. The lesson is that we expect coupons to do double duty. We want them not only to save us money but also to spare us the time and mental effort of working out how. In short, we respond to coupons automatically because they promise to relieve both our wallets and our minds.

One feature of a city street or square that is easy to overlook is how well it resists becoming obsolete over time. The ancient medieval squares of cities such as Marrakesh and Siena are still places where goods are sold every single day. What is sold there has changed enormously across the past five hundred years, yet the squares themselves carry on unchanged. A city square, like a shopping street, is therefore a remarkably durable technology, even in an age dominated by online shopping. The very same shop that once sold buggy whips and typewriters might today repair cracked phones and serve bubble tea. In other words, one fixed set of physical structures quietly supports a stream of constantly evolving uses. Jane Jacobs, the great prophet of the city economy, made much of this point in her writings. She correctly foresaw that the city would persist, contradicting those who claimed the Internet would bring about its death.

The genomics revolution finally let scientists see, at a molecular level, just how powerfully touch affects plants. Studying the genes of Arabidopsis thaliana, the laboratory workhorse of plant biology, researchers found that touch alone set off a dramatic response. That response reached deep into the plant's hormones and gene expression and could sharply hold back its growth. In their experiment, the scientists gently stroked the plants with soft paintbrushes and then read their genetic reactions. Within just thirty minutes of being touched, fully ten percent of the plant's genome had been altered. Clearly, the plant was reorganizing its priorities to deal with the disturbance. It was pulling energy away from the demanding task of growing taller. Touched again and again, the plant cut its upward growth rate by as much as thirty percent.

Evolution would grind to a halt only if nothing in the environment ever changed. But over the vast stretch of evolutionary time, the conditions almost always do change. An ice age may begin, the average rainfall may shift, or the prevailing winds may move. Because such changes keep occurring, evolution does not actually stop; instead it constantly tracks the shifting environment. Suppose the average temperature of an area drifts steadily downward over many centuries. Then successive generations of animals will be pushed by selection pressure toward growing longer coats of hair. If the temperature later reverses and creeps upward again, a new selection pressure takes over. Under that new pressure, the same animals are nudged back toward shorter coats.

When we look at a work of art and try to decide whether we recognize and understand its content, the act is not purely visual. It is also a mental process, built largely on the elements we can identify and categorize within and around the work. As we look and think, clues arise from where the work is, when it was made, what culture produced it, and who created it. Any information we can gather helps us grasp the work's context. That context covers the historical, social, personal, political, or scientific reasons the work was made. Using all the contextual information we have collected, we then interpret what the work means. Understanding art, in this view, depends on far more than the eye. It is an interpretive act that leans heavily on the knowledge we bring to the picture.

It is tempting to believe that if every part is excellent, the whole must be excellent too. Yet this assumption ignores something essential: how the parts behave together. A startup staffed entirely by efficient people may still fail if those people misjudge who is responsible for what. When two capable specialists each assume the other will handle a task, the task simply falls through the cracks. A unit of good people can be trapped on a hopeless project, and a project of good ideas can drift without a center. Therefore, judging a team only by the quality of its members is not enough. We ought to treasure this fact rather than overlook it, for it is a remarkable gift. The farther the source of the light, the further back in time we are able to look. Many of the barriers to trade exist not because of a lack of markets or customers, but because there are major barriers to getting products to market at competitive prices. Transaction costs are significant for companies — not only the straight exchange costs, but also the cost of converting, paying, and hedging funds just to pay for the goods and services. Having a common currency means that many of those transaction costs disappear and the savings can be reinvested back into firms' productivity and innovation. Basically, useless costs turn into productive costs — with longer-term benefits to the whole economy. By unifying some of the currencies, whole economies benefit and grow more than they would as independents. So a common currency provides for a strong economic foundation that all can benefit from.
The money saved by a common currency can be back into firms' productivity and innovation.

The renowned British philosopher Alfred North Whitehead asserted that "civilization advances by extending the number of operations we can perform without thinking about them." Take, for example, the "advance" offered to civilization by the discount coupon, which allows consumers to assume that they will receive a reduced purchase price by presenting the coupon. The extent to which we have learned to operate mechanically on that assumption is illustrated in the experience of one automobile-tire company. Mailed-out coupons that — because of a printing error — offered no savings to recipients produced just as much customer response as did error-free coupons that offered substantial savings. The obvious but instructive point here is that we expect discount coupons to do double duty. Not only do we expect them to save us money, we also expect them to save us the time and mental energy required to think about how to do it. In today's world, we need the first advantage to handle pocketbook strain; but we need the second advantage to handle something potentially more important — brain strain.

Innovative high-tech products tend to show a low price elasticity of demand. This means that raising or lowering the price changes their sales far less than it would for ordinary goods. The reason lies with the buyers who come first. Early adopters care less about the price than about a product's performance and novelty. Because they crave the newest capabilities, cutting the price does little to expand demand. A high price may even work in the product's favor by signaling quality and prestige. Evolution will come to a standstill until something in the conditions changes: the onset of an ice age, a change in the average rainfall of the area, a shift in the prevailing wind. Such changes do happen when we are dealing with a timescale as long as the evolutionary one. As a consequence, evolution normally does not come to a halt, but constantly tracks the changing environment. If there is a steady downward drift in the average temperature in the area, a drift that persists over centuries, successive generations of animals will be propelled by a steady selection 'pressure' in the direction, say, of growing longer coats of hair. If after a few thousand years of reduced temperature the trend reverses and average temperatures creep up again, the animals will come under the influence of a new selection pressure, and will be pushed towards growing shorter coats again.
Because the conditions keep changing, evolution does not come to a halt but constantly the changing environment.

The process we go through when we look at a work of art to determine if we recognize and can make sense of its content is not just a visual one. It is a mental process as well, largely based on the elements within and about the work we can identify and categorize. As we look and think, we may be given clues about what the work means by where it is, when it was made, what culture it came from, who created it, or why it was made. We should strive to understand a work of art as we see it, without being influenced by the background of the work, its creator, or its historical context. Any information we can gather helps us understand the work's context, that is, for what historical, social, personal, political, or scientific reasons the work of art was made. And then, using all the contextual information we have gathered, we interpret the work of art's content to discover what it means or symbolizes.

The fact that ...(~라는 사실), drive + 목적어 + to부정사(~가 …하도록 몰아가다), alternative sources of income(대체 수입원).
343 41번 요약 단어 정답 서술형
정답: (A) innovation / (B) diversify
(A) 비싼 유가는 기술 '혁신(innovation)'을 촉진한다. (B) 유가 하락 위협은 생산자를 '다각화하게(diversify)' 만든다.
344 43번 배열 영작 정답 서술형
정답: Anna mentioned that despite having limited space she enjoyed taking care of her plants.
mentioned that 명사절, despite + 동명사(having), enjoy + 동명사(taking care of) 구조.
345 43번 조건 영작 정답 서술형
정답: The letter inspired her to plant herbs again.
inspire + 목적어(her) + to부정사(to plant)의 5형식. again으로 '다시'를 표현.
346 43번 우리말 해석 정답 서술형
정답: 그 쪽지에서 Pike 부인은 남편을 잃은 후 정원 가꾸기를 포기했었다고 밝혔다.
had given up(대과거, 밝힌 시점보다 이전), give up + 동명사(gardening), after losing(전치사 + 동명사).
